Plus: Space gets "spicier" | Thursday, October 22, 2026

Axios Future of Defense
By Thomas Novelly · Oct 22, 2026

Happy Friday's eve, y'all! A few quick items:

  • 🛰️ ICYMI: Project Omega and Charter Space are researching how radioactive isotopes can keep satellites safely in orbit longer. More on that here.
  • 🎤 I'll be onstage next month for the Axios Future of Defense Summit! Check out our speakers and request an invite here.

🌎 Watch this space: Let's dive into an exclusive on Russia's approach toward a key U.S. satellite, chat with True Anomaly's CEO and get an update on the Space Force's role in the Middle East.

Today's newsletter is 1,623 words, a 6-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: 📸 Exclusive: Russia stalks U.S. satellite
 

A new space photo shows a Russian satellite (right) less than a mile from ICEYE X36 (left) on Oct. 17. Photo: Vantor
 

A new, exclusive image shared with Axios shows a Russian satellite bearing down on a U.S.-owned spacecraft during a tense orbital incident last week.

Why it matters: The photo, snapped by spatial intelligence company Vantor, shows how commercial satellites are already becoming possible targets for stalking, jamming and, potentially, space weapons in geopolitical conflicts.

  • "This image captures a reality long recognized by our national security leaders — space is becoming increasingly contested," Vantor CEO Dan Smoot told me in an exclusive statement.
  • "Seeing one spacecraft repeatedly maneuver close to another raises serious concerns about capability and intent," he said.

The big picture: Private sector firms like Vantor are filling the information gap as the U.S. military's classified space capabilities make it difficult for the government to share intelligence with the public.

  • The Defense Department declined to provide Axios details on Russia's space maneuvers. A State Department official made a brief statement on the matter yesterday.

How it happened: As the Russian satellite maneuvered into an alarming position, firms like Vantor, which captures space and Earth imaging, and LeoLabs, which tracks orbital objects, were closely watching.

  • On Saturday, Vantor captured the Russian Cosmos 2612 satellite stalking the U.S. commercial ICEYE-X36 as both vehicles orbited Earth at speeds around 17,000 mph.
  • LeoLabs provided Axios a detailed report on Friday of how Cosmos 2612 closed a gap of nearly 250 miles to get within roughly one-third of a mile from the U.S. satellite.

"Without that transparency that we get from companies, we'd all be in the dark," Clayton Swope, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told me. "I don't think we'd have a really good picture about, when the rubber meets the road, what these threats look like in space."

State of play: ICEYE has a space-based network that has supported Ukraine's military.

  • Experts told me Russia's willingness to burn its own satellite's fuel and rapidly change its altitude, orbital plane and speed to catch up to ICEYE-X36 was alarming and potentially dangerous.
  • LeoLabs said the Russian satellite began drifting away from ICEYE on Sunday, easing tensions.

What they're saying: LeoLabs and Vantor said that this transparency is crucial to protect the space infrastructure the U.S. relies on.

  • "Knowing where objects are and what they're doing is essential for any operator to distinguish routine activity from anomalous behavior that may put their spacecraft at risk," said LeoLabs spokesperson Victoria Heath.
  • "By using satellites to capture images of other spacecraft in orbit, we can better understand how they're operating and identify potentially concerning activity," Smoot told me.

ICEYE, however, hasn't said much about the incident.

  • The company told Axios in an emailed statement on Monday that it's tracking the situation and that its "constellation architecture is designed for continuity and resilience."

The bottom line: The commercial images and intelligence show how U.S. adversaries may target key satellites in future conflicts in the absence of well-defined norms and widespread transparency.

  • "If you look at the spectrum of conflict, it's not wartime but it's not pure peacetime," Swope said. "There is no real understanding of what is hostile, what is escalatory."
 
 
2. Exclusive: Space will get "spicier"
 

True Anomaly participated in the Space Force's Victus Haze demo this summer. Photo: Courtesy of True Anomaly
 

Space warfare is "only going to get spicier from here," True Anomaly CEO Even Rogers told me in an interview.

  • True Anomaly, a defense tech startup specializing in space defense and satellite security, participated in a Space Force demo in July in which its spacecraft pursued and targeted a Rocket Lab satellite.

Why it matters: That demo, dubbed Victus Haze, is an early sign of what orbital warfare will probably look like, Rogers said.

Yes, but: The industry is changing fast. "We're in the same place that aviation was in the 1930s," Rogers said.

  • "Space is going through the same transformation that air went through," he said, adding that we'll probably look back at operations like Victus Haze as "seminal moments."

Threat level: Demos like this one are becoming more urgent, as the Russia-U.S. satellite tango over the weekend shows.

Catch up quick: In Victus Haze, the Space Force tasked Rocket Lab to launch its maneuverable space vehicle, Puma, in 24 hours. Once in orbit, True Anomaly's spacecraft, Jackal, quickly chased it down.

  • True Anomaly said it was the first ever space-to-space pursuit as part of a "tactically responsive" Space Force demo.

Inside the room: Rogers said the True Anomaly team worked quickly on the operations floor to jockey Jackal into a position around Rocket Lab's Puma spacecraft.

  • "We were making upgrades to the Jackal [software] platform between sorties and during the mission," Rogers said.

What we're watching: Future rapid Space Force demos are on the horizon.

  • Another upcoming mission, Victus Sol, will use Firefly Aerospace's Alpha rocket.
 
 
3. SPACECENT's growth
 

Guardians with the 162nd Electromagnetic Warfare Combat Detachment work on an antenna in November 2024. Photo: Violette Hosack/DVIDS
 

The number of troops focused on Middle East space operations will likely expand "fivefold" in the coming years, a top Space Force general said this week.

Why it matters: The Space Force is the smallest service, but it's playing a big role in Iran.

What he's saying: "I would expect we'd be about fivefold the size we are today," Brig. Gen. Todd J. Benson, the Space Forces Central commander, said during a Mitchell Institute webinar on Monday.

Zoom in: Space Forces Central, or SPACECENT, was established in 2022 with just 21 Guardians and civilians overseeing mission planning and space operations.

  • Benson said his small Space Forces Central staff will likely grow over the next three or so years for planning, cyber and intelligence needs.

Zoom out: Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine said in March that space forces disrupted "Iran's ability to see, communicate and respond" during Operation Epic Fury.

  • Benson said the Space Force also assisted in the herculean rescue operation of a downed airman over Iran in April.

 "The effects that we provided [created] extra time for that rescue team to do what they needed to do," Benson said of that mission. "I know without a shadow of a doubt, without that, the outcome could have been completely different."

The bottom line: The Space Force is being woven into more military operations.

  • Axios first reported that the service created its own Special Operations headquarters to further integrate the Space Force into future high-level missions.

4. Motor madness
By Colin Demarest
 

A Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System is fired during the Koolendong exercise in Australia. Photo: Colton K. Garrett/DVIDS
 

A newly minted L3Harris Technologies facility in Arkansas will consolidate solid-rocket motor production and help double capacity for work on GMLRS, rocket artillery made by Lockheed Martin.

Why it matters: Propulsion and energetics have long been a chokepoint for the U.S. — and the military is now facing tough questions about the state of its munitions stockpile and industry's ability to quickly refill it.

Driving the news: L3Harris cut the ribbon on the 60,000-square-foot factory in Camden this week. The company's president for missile solutions, Ken Bedingfield, told me it serves as a "blueprint" for ongoing expansions.

  • "This is one of the highest quantity motors that we produce," he said, adding that the company is "moving on a wartime footing" and "investing ahead of need."

Zoom in: The new plant features robotics throughout — moving materiel from station to station — along with automated casting, curing and X-ray inspection cells.

Zoom out: The preexisting L3Harris footprint in Camden includes 100-plus buildings across 2,000 acres.

  • Workers there produce more than 115,000 solid-rocket motors of various sizes annually.

The bottom line: "Rocket propulsion is a vital national security capability," Pentagon chief weapons buyer Michael Duffey said in a statement provided to reporters.

5. Quick hits
 

Varda's W-1 vehicle after landing in 2024. Photo: Varda/John Kraus
 

💫 Elon Musk reportedly ordered the Starlink connection Ukraine's military relies on to be slowed down, according to the Wall Street Journal.

  • Yes, but: Reuters reported a few days earlier that the order came from within the White House.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: There's still a lot of finger pointing and, as Axios' Barak Ravid has reported, the situation was "still unclear" to the Ukrainians last week.

🔎 Varda Space Industries is probing how microgravity could improve a new cancer treatment, my colleague Alex Fitzpatrick reports.

  • Context: "Microgravity lets pharmaceutical compounds crystalize without disruptive processes like sedimentation and convection, potentially leading to better solubility, efficacy and other benefits," Fitzpatrick writes.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: It's a fascinating experiment that weaves together two of the hottest sectors right now, biotech and space.

🇮🇱 The Israel Defense Forces has a new space warfare commander, the Times of Israel reports.

  • What they're saying: Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said the country's new space division will turn "Israel into a security space power: Star Wars, made in Israel," the newspaper reports.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Given the heavy use of U.S. space assets in the Middle East, the move isn't surprising.
 
 
6. Check this out
 

A piece of potential space debris landed in a Minnesota cornfield last week. Photo: Stevens County Sheriff's Office
 

Talk about an October surprise.

Zoom in: The Stevens County Sheriff's Office in Minnesota got a call on Oct. 14 about foreign debris and later confirmed that a "large, metallic object, approximately 11-feet in diameter, presumably a space object" was found in a local cornfield, according to a news release on the agency's Facebook page.

Zoom out: China's Zhuque-2E rocket launched from the Gobi Desert last month. Ars Technica reports the object could be debris from that mission.
